claims.text: Ultra-rapid quenching of a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy at more than 1×10^5 K/s can produce an amorphous structure.
Melt spinning can achieve cooling rates in the range of 10^5–10^6 K/s.
The ultra-rapidly quenched alloy will have at least twice the critical casting thickness of an otherwise comparable conventionally cast alloy.
The ultra-rapidly quenched alloy will have a crystallization onset temperature 20–30 K higher than the slower-cooled baseline.
Minimizing oxygen contamination is required for the predicted enhancement.
Superheating the melt sufficiently above its liquidus is required for the predicted enhancement.
Uniform cooling across the sample cross-section avoids partial crystallization.
Rapid quenching promotes high mixing entropy in the undercooled liquid.
Rapid quenching impedes diffusion-limited growth of crystalline nuclei.
Phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance the glass-forming ability of the studied phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy.
Phosphorus and multiple principal elements stabilize the amorphous state against subsequent crystallization.
Cooling at approximately 52 K/s yields a complex crystalline microstructure, whereas melt spinning at 10^5–10^6 K/s yields an amorphous structure in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Cooling rates below approximately 10^4 K/s are an appropriate conventional-casting baseline.
Insufficient cooling rate will reduce or eliminate amorphous-phase formation.
Improper superheat control or high oxygen contamination will reduce or eliminate the enhancement in glass formation and thermal stability.
The magnitude of the improvement will vary among phosphorus-containing alloy chemistries.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is explicitly conditioned on sufficient and uniform cooling, yet the falsification rule treats partial crystallization caused by nonuniform or insufficient cooling as falsification. Such a result violates the stated applicability conditions rather than decisively testing the conditional hypothesis.
